title: Sukkot: Ecclesiastes
hook: Ecclesiastes, with its hard truths about time, is read in the season of joy
tomorrow: Sukkot: the season of our joy (Deuteronomy 16:14–15)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ushpizin, guests from the past. Your line was invite the guests. Did a real invitation go out? Today, a guest of a different kind: a book that sits down at the festival table and says something uncomfortable. Day six hundred sixty.

The harvest is in. The sukkah is decorated. People are eating outside under the branches. And on the Shabbat of Sukkot, in many synagogues, the reader stands up and chants a book that opens like this: "Vanity of vanities, saith Koheleth; vanity of vanities, all is vanity." Everything is fleeting. Nothing lasts. What's the point of all your work? It sounds like the wrong book for the week. It was chosen on purpose.
screen: `THE HARVEST IS IN.` → `VANITY OF VANITIES.` → `THE WRONG BOOK, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: The book is Ecclesiastes. In Hebrew, Kohelet, the name its speaker gives himself. Readers often take it as one who gathers, or one who speaks to a gathering. He calls himself the son of David, king in Jerusalem, and tradition identifies him with King Solomon. And the word translated vanity, hevel, is the Hebrew word for breath, vapor. Not worthless, exactly. Fleeting. Like breath on a cold morning: there, then gone. Kohelet looks hard at life. You come into the world with nothing and leave with nothing. The wise die like fools. You work, and someone else inherits it. There's nothing new under the sun. And then he says: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." A time to be born, a time to die, a time to weep, a time to laugh. Why read this at Sukkot? Several reasons are given. One is that Sukkot is the harvest festival, when people feel richest and most secure, and Kohelet is a reminder not to mistake the barns for forever. Another: the sukkah itself teaches the same lesson. You leave your solid house to sit in a hut that a wind could knock over. And Kohelet doesn't end in despair. Again and again he comes back to joy: "Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart." Enjoy life with the people you love, he says, all the fleeting days. That's the paradox. Joy isn't the opposite of knowing things pass. It may be the right response to it. The festival keeps its eyes open. Sephardi communities generally don't read the book publicly; many Ashkenazi ones do.
screen: `KOHELET: THE ONE WHO GATHERS.` · `HEVEL: BREATH, VAPOR.` · `A TIME TO EVERY PURPOSE.` · `EAT THY BREAD WITH JOY.` · then, large: `JOY WITH OPEN EYES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line of Ecclesiastes. Take this one: a time to weep, and a time to laugh. Say it slowly, twice. Then think of something good in your life right now that won't last forever: a child's age, a friendship in its easy season, the light this time of year. Hold it, knowing it's fleeting, and let yourself enjoy it anyway, maybe more because of that. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Kohelet. Ecclesiastes. The book of breath and fleeting things, read in the season of joy, which still tells you to eat your bread with joy.
Your line: joy with open eyes. Today, enjoy one ordinary pleasure fully, knowing it will pass. Day six hundred sixty.

howItsDone: In many Ashkenazi synagogues the book of Ecclesiastes (Kohelet) is read on the Shabbat during Sukkot, or on Shemini Atzeret when no Shabbat falls in the intermediate days; Sephardi communities generally do not read it publicly.

myth: it means breath or vapor: fleeting, not worthless.
Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy.
every Jewish community reads Kohelet publicly on Sukkot

fork.setup: you're Kohelet. you've seen that wealth, wisdom and work all pass like breath. what's your advice?
options: eat your bread with joy, with the people you love.
fork.reveal: Kohelet comes back again and again to joy: enjoy life in its fleeting days.

original.note: Hebrew: Ecclesiastes; the one who gathers, from kahal, assembly.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy book that says nothing matters.
what it means: everything is breath, so eat your bread with joy, eyes open.
what a scholar hears: hevel as vapor, Kohelet from kahal, and the Ashkenazi custom of reading it on Sukkot.

notes: Ecclesiastes 1:2, 3:1 and 9:7 (JPS 1917) quoted from memory; verify wording (JPS 1917 spells 'Koheleth').
Reasons for reading Kohelet on Sukkot (harvest and security; the impermanent sukkah; joy) are traditional explanations from various authorities; not one source.
Kohelet's identification with Solomon is traditional; the meaning 'gatherer' is the common derivation.
Practice paraphrases Ecclesiastes 3:4 ('a time to weep, and a time to laugh') without quotation marks.
